en: The monk Kāśyapa questioned the Teacher, the Joy of the Śākyas:
"O Lord, is there any evil for the Noble Ones when they exercise sovereign power?
In the presence of Kāśyapa, the Teacher, the Leader of the World, spoke.
Listen, Kāśyapa, to the hundredth [offense] consisting of the exercise of authority over monks:
whoever seeks to exercise authority over the Saṅgha of the four quarters that is free from deceit.
That wicked monk is cooked in hell for twenty eons.
Having passed away from there, that deluded soul is born among the hungry ghosts;
intent on devouring excrement, he remains there for ten million eons.
If a monk established in the training should wish to go to hell,
he should exercise lordship for even a single moment in a temple of the Jina.
He who exercises mastery over many noble ones— [5] [he shall go to hell].
He plays in the forest of hell with a thousand black serpents.
Among men, the Caṇḍāla is the lowest; among women, the prostitute is the most base.
Even more so than these is he who is the master over noble monks.
He is not to be touched, nor spoken to, nor saluted by lay followers;
out of compassion for that sinner, a funeral offering (piṇḍa) should be given to him alone.
But whoever shall burn this sinner, who has committed an act of immediate retribution—
Even he who is base and exceedingly wretched, born into low wombs,
a sinner who treats the Teacher and the Lord of the Saṅgha like a red-hot iron ball—
his only destination below is the state of existence in the ocean of hell.
[11] But as for those monks who have generated the thought of awakening and are endowed with virtuous conduct—
what conscious being on earth could exercise sovereignty over them?
Worthy of veneration by the world including its gods, the supreme among assemblies—
whoever approaches this moving stūpa attains the ultimate state beyond the world.
[12] Attaining the ultimate state beyond the world.
As long as stupas consisting of merit remain on earth as moving monuments,
so long is the teaching of the Sage honored in the world including the gods.
The stationary stupa of the Sage is always worshiped with devotion by the wise.
Having relied upon the moving stūpa, the Leader of the World has attained parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, whoever [honors] the Teacher’s moving stūpa, adorned with the ornament of ethical discipline—
The foolish and sinful person destroys [the merit of] those who have committed the immediate transgressions (ānantarya).
Within food, the mobile body of the Lord of Munis is sustained by the mobile stūpa.
That evil-minded person who violates the dwelling place honored by the three worlds [is cast there].
Even he who should subject a monk— though that monk be of immoral conduct— to imprisonment or flogging,
is himself sawn apart with saws by the rākṣasas of Yama.
The Teacher has praised giving even to oneself, and to the Saṅgha;
give to the Gautama Saṅgha, for what is given to the Saṅgha yields great fruit. He is worthy of veneration throughout the three worlds, and he is a great lake of merit.
For what wise person would desire the sovereignty over that foremost of assemblies?
[19] As for the sinner who seeks to stand at the head of the highest assembly, the fire of his own sin will soon consume his body. [20]
A wise ascetic should not exercise authority over even a single person;
for by the mere corruption of the mind, he will certainly go to hell.
Like a fire with a mass of brilliance, it is like a cluster of flickering sparks.
In the same way, a wise person should always revere a monk endowed with virtue.
A man who is a mass of splendor when satisfied, when enraged destroys a man with a single stroke of his sword.

A monk endowed with ethical discipline destroys the three worlds with the sword of his curse. But he of afflicted intellect who corrupts a monk adorned with the excellent jewel of the training shall burn in hell, wailing, for one eon.
"This monk of broken discipline speaks; who here is so reckless?

The "reckless" one (*sāhasin*) is of four kinds, declared by the Sage to be like the mango fruit (*cūtaphala*). [25] In another [version], it is "the reckless one" (*sāhasī*); [this refers to] moral conduct (*śīla*).
The wise ascetic should not corrupt the character of one who is conscious;
even if that person is ill-behaved, he should not be called so, for this is the domain of the Omniscient One regarding ethical conduct.
A wise person who desires their own accomplishment should not corrupt the mind of one who has taken up the thought of awakening and who has gone for refuge to the Three Jewels.
This is especially true if that person is a monk who truly abides in the vows of training.
How could one generate the thought of enlightenment that is so contrary to ascetics?
One who is adorned with the vows of training should never harbor a malicious mind toward ascetics if they seek their own welfare.
The wrath of one who possesses virtuous conduct could swiftly incinerate even the three worlds.
When pleased, they bestow favor; when enraged, they bring fear with their curses.
Therefore, those seeking their own welfare should always honor ascetics.
A minister who is powerful through his spells, when satisfied, brings about prosperity step by step;
but when enraged, he destroys utterly by means of the inconceivable power of his spells.
Even for a monk whose moral conduct has failed, one with a defiled mind... [31]
The monk exercises lordship and is reborn as a black cobra;
having seized a hundred yojanas, his movement proceeds,
and he is struck on the head by crows with sharp iron beaks.
That which constantly flows from him— pus, blood, and gore—
is prepared as the very food for that sinful one by his own past actions; indeed,
it is through his actions regarding food.

That wise person by whom the eightfold vow has been undertaken for the sake of awakening is always to be venerated by the virtuous; one should not disparage him, even if he were considered an enemy here on earth or even the moon.
[35] Even if he acts as an enemy here, he is still to be honored.
One who has undertaken the precepts would surely be loathed by the whole world.
Even if the body were burnt, one should not corrupt the mind;
but when the body possesses consciousness, one should certainly not corrupt the ascetic.
Those of immoral conduct, performers of cruel deeds, most wicked, and destined for hell—
these false monks will exercise authority over the noble ones.
Even for a moment, they will maintain their dominance over the community.
"Monks, they are even born into the womb of a dog, O Kāśyapa.
Noble one, regarding a being who is desired, or even toward an enemy, O Kāśyapa, let not even a single thought of malice arise for anyone, even for the duration of a finger-snap. [39–40]
What is the use of saying more here? One who holds authority over the Saṅgha commits a sin;
for it has been taught by the Sage that through skillful means one incurs the sequence of the immediate (ānantarya) offenses. [41]
Enough, O Lord! It is sufficient for me; having heard this much, fear arises within me.
This supreme speech, honored by the world including the gods, is concluded.
The fourth chapter, the Kāśyapaparipṛcchāsūtra, is finished.
